historical_timeline.summary: Begins publishing under the pen name Pablo Neruda.
Begins a series of consular posts in Asia and later in Buenos Aires, Barcelona and Madrid (to 1935).
A court judgment changes his birth name to Pablo Neruda.
The Senate approves his appointment as ambassador to France.
Health problems begin; operated on for prostate cancer in France.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Resigns as ambassador and returns to Chile.
Dies at the Clínica Santa María in Santiago, twelve days after the military coup; the death certificate gives cancer cachexia.
Chile's medical legal service reports no relevant chemical substances in his exhumed remains.
An international forensic panel rejects cachexia as the cause of death without naming a cause.
Clostridium botulinum DNA reported in a molar and bone; how it got there could not be determined.
The Santiago appeals court orders the investigation reopened.

claims.statement: In October 2017 an international panel of 16 forensic experts said it was certain he had not died of cancer cachexia, as the death certificate stated; one member said there was no indication of cachexia and that he was obese at the time of death. The panel said it could neither exclude nor affirm a natural or violent cause of death, and reported potentially deadly bacteria in a sample from one of his molars.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after his death; one part of the dispute over the cause of death. The panel's statement that he was not wasted at death is consistent with a man who was not cachectic; it is not used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Whether he died of his prostate cancer, of another natural cause such as an infection, or of poisoning is disputed and unresolved. The death certificate gives cancer cachexia; the 2013 tests found no relevant chemical substances; the 2017 panel rejected cachexia without naming a cause; the 2023 finding of Clostridium botulinum could not show how it got there; and the investigation was reopened in 2024.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The record takes neither side. The cause of death is not used in the modern episode, which is set two years before his death and does not foreshadow it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: De novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a 66-year-old Chilean poet and diplomat posted abroad, on the NCCN prostate cancer guideline, the AUA/SUO advanced prostate cancer guideline and the CMID prostate cancer monograph. Urinary symptoms and bone pain with a hard prostate and a raised PSA lead to MRI, an MRI-targeted biopsy, conventional staging (CT and bone scan) and PSMA PET/CT; the disease is classified as low volume, and the choice is continuous androgen deprivation with apalutamide plus radiotherapy to the prostate, without docetaxel. The episode covers flare protection, early PSA response and the three-month PSA, germline and somatic testing, bone health (DXA, FRAX, vitamin D, calcium, exercise, a dental check and denosumab at the osteoporosis dose), the cardiometabolic risks of androgen deprivation, apalutamide's drug interaction with amlodipine, its rash and its effect on thyroid function, hot flashes, sexual health, fatigue, mood, and care in Spanish, his first language, around his writing and diplomatic work. His documented prostate cancer, operated on in France in July 1971 while he was ambassador, frames the episode; the dispute over his death two years later is history only.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Neruda returns two weeks after his first visit, with a professional Spanish interpreter. In the past ten days he had an MRI of the prostate, a targeted biopsy at the urology practice, a CT scan, a bone scan and a PSMA PET/CT. The results were explained to him this morning by Dr. Okonkwo-Lund of medical oncology and again today: prostate cancer, Gleason 4+4, that has spread to two lymph nodes in the pelvis and to two places in the bones, the right hip bone and the lowest lumbar vertebra, with nothing in the lungs, liver or other organs. He chose, after hearing the options, to start apalutamide today, with a leuprolide injection in one week and radiotherapy to the prostate in about six weeks. His blood was drawn today for germline genetic testing after counseling. He had his bone density scan this morning. The right hip pain is a little better on acetaminophen, 5 of 10 at worst, and still wakes him some nights; he has no leg weakness, numbness, or change in bladder or bowel control. His urinary symptoms are unchanged. He feels the news is hard but says he would rather know. He wants to keep writing every morning and to continue his duties.

assessment.assessment: The diagnosis is confirmed. By the conventional-imaging definition used in the trials and the AUA/SUO guideline, high volume means four or more bone metastases with at least one outside the spine and pelvis, or visceral metastases; he has two bone metastases, both within the spine and pelvis, and no visceral disease, so the disease is low volume. The PSMA PET/CT shows nothing more. He has symptoms from the bone metastasis in the right ilium

Androgen deprivation should be combined with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor. Apalutamide, enzalutamide, darolutamide and abiraterone with prednisone are all reasonable. Apalutamide is a single daily tablet without a steroid and improved survival in low-volume disease in the TITAN trial; abiraterone needs prednisone and can worsen blood pressure and glucose, which matters with his hypertension and prediabetes. Docetaxel is not recommended: in low-volume disease it did not clearly improve survival, and triplet therapy is reserved for selected patients with high-volume disease. Apalutamide started a week before the first leuprolide injection also blocks the testosterone flare, so bicalutamide is not needed

In low-volume metastatic disease, radiotherapy to the prostate added to androgen deprivation improved survival in STAMPEDE, and the guidelines support it in selected patients. It is recommended, about six weeks after starting androgen deprivation, as 55 Gy in 20 daily fractions

Bone-protective drugs at the monthly doses used to prevent skeletal events are recommended in castration-resistant disease; in hormone-sensitive disease, early zoledronic acid did not reduce skeletal events (CALGB 90202). His own fracture risk is the reason to treat: FRAX with androgen deprivation counted gives a hip fracture risk of 3.4 percent, above the 3 percent threshold. Denosumab 60 mg every six months, the osteoporosis dose, is recommended after a dental examination and once vitamin D replacement has begun and calcium is normal. The painful iliac metastasis is likely to settle on androgen deprivation; radiotherapy to that bone remains an option if it does not

Germline testing is recommended for every patient with metastatic prostate cancer, and somatic testing of the tumor for metastatic disease; the results could change later treatment (a PARP inhibitor for a BRCA2 alteration) and would matter for his relatives. Pre-test counseling was done today
Apalutamide is a strong CYP3A4 inducer and will lower amlodipine levels, so blood pressure may rise in the first weeks. It also raises the risk of rash, falls, fractures and raised TSH
